Nickel-Catalyzed Photoredox Allenylation of Alkyl Halides
Tingjun Hu,
§
Camille Beluze,
§
Vincent Fagué, Oho Eliantine Kambire, Didier Bouyssi,*
Nuno Monteiro,* and Abderrahmane Amgoune*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 9519−9524
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: We report a dual Ni/photoredox-catalyzed cross-coupling
method for propargyl carbonates and nonactivated alkyl bromides, facilitating
the synthesis of a variety of substituted allenes under mild and practical
conditions. Mechanistically, the reaction integrates Ni-catalyzed activation of
the propargyl electrophile via S
N
2
′ oxidative addition at Ni(I) with silyl radical-
induced activation of the alkyl halide through halogen-atom transfer. This
methodology provides a gentle approach for introducing allenyl groups into
complex halogenated aliphatic molecules, offering further opportunities for
derivatization.
A
llenes represent a highly versatile class of compounds
exhibiting unique physical and chemical properties.
1
These characteristics make allenes valuable building blocks in
organic synthesis,
2
contributing to the construction of larger
and structurally complex molecular targets, including natural
products, pharmaceuticals,
3
and advanced materials.
4
There-
fore, developing robust and mild strategies for the catalytic
allenylation of organic molecules remains a significant and
active area of research in synthetic chemistry.
5
Early
developments in transition metal-catalyzed allenylation
methods primarily focused on palladium-catalyzed S
N
2
′-type
nucleophilic substitution reactions of propargyl electrophiles.
6
However, these methods often face challenges such as poor
functional group tolerance when using highly reactive
organometallic nucleophiles, and regioselectivity issues on
possible formation of the isomeric propargylation products.
Despite substantial progress in developing efficient strategies
for the allenylation of unsaturated substrates, particularly
those involving C(sp
2
)-X bonds, the involvement of aliphatic
coupling partners in these processes remains challenging.
Alkyl halides are abundant and easily accessible precursors
of organometallic aliphatic carbons. The nucleophilic addition
of zinc or magnesium organometallics to propargyl electro-
philes has been well investigated under various transition
metal catalysts, including palladium, copper, iron,
7
and more
recently, nickel
8
(Scheme 1a). However, developing new
methods for the allenylation of nonactivated alkyl halides
through direct C(sp
3
)-X bond manipulation would be
exceptionally advantageous. Such methods would avoid
preparation and handling of air- and moisture-sensitive
organometallic reagents, allowing better functional group
tolerance and enabling the use of more complex organo-
halides.
To date, there is only one prior report by Wang describing
a nickel-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling of propargyl
electrophiles with nonactivated alkyl halides.
9
While this
protocol allows for the construction of a wide range of allenic
frameworks, it notably excludes all-aliphatic allenes and only
applies to alkyl iodide substrates, which are less attractive due
to their limited availability and stability compared to their
bromo- and chloro-counterparts. Additionally, this method
requires the use of excess of manganese metal as a reductant
and proceeds best in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, a less desirable
solvent in terms of sustainability and toxicity (Scheme 1b).
Herein, we report a nickel/photoredox dual catalytic
strategy for the selective allenylation of unactivated alkyl
bromides based on silyl radical-mediated halogen-atom
transfer (XAT) process (Scheme 1c).
10
In this approach, a
silane functions as both a XAT promoter and a reductive
quencher of the photocatalytic cycle. This method provides
facile access to diversely functionalized tri- and tetrasub-
stituted allenic compounds,
11
including all-aliphatic deriva-
tives, under very mild conditions without the need for air-free
techniques. Moreover, the reaction can be conducted in
acetone, a more sustainable and less toxic solvent. The
strategy also avoids the need for stoichiometric metal-based
reagents or reductants. A mechanistic rationale for the cross-
electrophile coupling reaction is provided.
Preliminary studies focused on the cross-coupling of 4-
bromo-tetrahydro-2H-pyran (1a) with alk-2-ynyl carbonate
(2a) in the presence of a stoichiometric amount of
(TMS)
3
SiH,
12
as a model reaction (Table 1). First
experiments led to the identification of nickel(II)Cl
2

iridium complex Ir[(dF(CF

(0.5 mol %)
proved to be a suitable photocatalyst for this transformation
under the irradiation of a 40 W blue LED lamp (455 nm) at
50% light intensity.
13
Control experiments confirmed that the
dual catalytic system, light irradiation, and silane are essential
for this transformation (Table 1, entries 2−6). A base was
also required (Table 1, entry 7), with sodium carbonate (1
equiv) being the most effective. Finally, acetone was selected
as a suitable and sustainable solvent (0.07 M). Under these
conditions, the corresponding allene (3) was produced in
84% spectroscopic yield within 24 h. Other bipyridine ligands
(L
2
, L
3
) and organophotocatalysts (e.g. 4-CzIPN and DPA)
showed lower performance at similar catalyst loadings (Table
1, entries 8−12). Amine base, such as triethylamine, failed to
promote the reaction. Instead, the corresponding allenic
reduction product
14
was obtained selectively (Table 1, entry
13). Finally, we identified the OBoc group as possible
alternative leaving group, while the OAc group showed much
lower efficiency (Table 1, entries 14−15).
The scope of the reaction was then investigated across a
series of propargyl carbonates and readily available alkyl
halides (Table 2). The transformation was effective with
primary and secondary nonactivated alkyl bromides bearing
various functional groups, such as alkene, ether, free alcohol,
amine, ester, nitrile, aryl chloride, and fluoroalkyl (3−20).
Notably, alkyl bromides performed better than their chloro-
and iodo-counterparts, as demonstrated in the synthesis of
allene (15) using different cyclohexyl halides. The cyclohexyl
allene was obtained in 1%, 71%, and 5% NMR yields, from
the iodo-, bromo-, and chloro-alkyl coupling partner,
respectively.
15
However, activated benzyl halides were an
exception. While benzyl bromides faced challenges in the
allenylation process, the more desirable and readily available
benzylic chlorides proved better coupling partners, as
illustrated in the synthesis of benzylic allene (13). Note-
worthily, tertiary bromides, e.g. tert-butyl bromide and 1-
bromoadamantane, did not participate in the coupling
reaction.
The allenylation of more complex organohalides was also
successful. A galactopyranose-derived bromide was cross-
coupled to yield the desired allenyl derivative (19) in 50%
yield. Additionally, a clofibric acid bromoalkyl ester was
allenylated in 63% yield (20), withstanding the interchange of

The scope of propargyl carbonates was further investigated.
Tertiary carbonate derivatives with electron-poor or electron-
rich aryl substituents (21−28) performed equally well.
Noteworthily, an ortho substituent on the aryl rings had a
detrimental effect on the reaction efficiency, delivering the
desired allene in low yield (29). Alkyl substituents on the
alkyne were also tolerated yielding all-aliphatic allenes in fair
yields (30−31 and 33−34). Secondary propargyl carbonates
also participated in the coupling reaction, affording
trisubstituted allenes in satisfying yields (32−33). Notably,
the dtbbpy ligand (L
2
) was more effective than L
1
in
promoting these reactions. Unfortunately, the more challeng-
ing primary carbonate (34) afforded only a low yield of the
desired terminal allene (23% yield, 70% conversion).
Similarly, the reaction with a terminal propargylic electrophile
(35) resulted in a low yield of the coupling product (10%
yield, full conversion). In both cases, the consumption of
starting materials was largely accompanied by degradation
rather than productive coupling.
Finally, to elucidate the reaction mechanism, we conducted
several mechanistic experiments (see the Supporting In-
formation for details). The reaction was anticipated to
proceed through oxidative addition of the propargyl
carbonate to nickel, capture of the alkyl radical, and
subsequent reductive elimination. We first investigated the
nature and oxidation state of the low-valent nickel species
purportedly promoting the oxidative addition of the propargyl
carbonate. For that purpose, we first evaluated the perform-
ance of zerovalent nickel as a catalyst in the synthesis of
allene 16. For instance, under standard conditions, using 1.5
mol % of Ni(COD)
2
/L
1
as catalyst, the reaction afforded
allene 16 in only 25% yield, demonstrating the lower
efficiency of zerovalent nickel catalyst in promoting the
coupling process.
16
Next, cyclic voltammetry (CV) studies were conducted to
gain further insights into the nickel species responsible for
the activation of the propargyl carbonate (2a). The cyclic
voltammogram of NiCl
2

addition of several equivalents of propargyl carbonate (2a) (5
and 10 equiv) resulted in an increased current at the first
reduction peak Ni(II)/Ni(I) along with a complete loss of

reversibility. This finding suggests a facile oxidative addition
of the propargyl carbonate to photogenerated Ni(I) species.
To confirm the involvement of a radical process, 2,2,6,6-
tetramethylpiperidinyloxy (TEMPO) was added into the
model reaction, which completely suppressed product
formation. However, we were unable to observe any
TEMPO-adduct. In addition, a radical clock experiment was
performed using cyclopropyl methyl bromide as a coupling
partner, which provided the alkenyl allene derivative (36) as
the sole coupling product, indicating the ring opening of a
cyclopropyl methyl radical to but-3-enyl radical (eq 1).
Based on documented studies and our observations, the
following sequence of events may be proposed as a possible
reaction mechanism. The (TMS)
3
SiH (E

(A)] = +0.73 V vs SCE)
17
would undergo direct
oxidative scission of the Si−H bond by the strongly oxidizing
photoexcited Ir(III)* photocatalyst (E
1/2
red
[Ir(III)*/Ir(II)] =
+1.21 V vs SCE)
18
in the presence of a base to generate a
(TMS)
3
Si radical intermediate (B). This radical would then
abstract the bromine atom from the organic halide, yielding
the corresponding nucleophilic alkyl radical.
19,20
Concur-
rently, a low-valent Ni(I) species (C), formed via the
photocatalytic single-electron reduction of the bipyridyl NiCl
2
precatalyst, would undergo S
N
2
′ oxidative addition of the
propargyl carbonate to generate allenyl-Ni(III) species (D).
Subsequently, single electron reduction of this high-valent Ni
species is proposed to occur via comproportionation with the
remaining Ni(I), yielding the corresponding allenylNi(II)
complex (E).
21
Capture of the alkyl radical by the Ni(II)
species, followed by reductive elimination of the desired alkyl
allene from Ni(III) species (F) would recycle Ni(I) (Scheme
2). The involvement of Ni(0) species instead of Ni(I) species
remains a possibility and could not be completely ruled out.
Evidence supporting the involvement of (TMS)
3
SiH in
bromine abstraction from the alkyl halide was obtained
through the detection of methoxytris(trimethylsilyl)silane as a
coproduct of the reaction (via GC-MS). This likely arises
from nucleophilic substitution of the silyl bromide by
methoxide anion released in the reaction medium.
22
In conclusion, we have developed a new dual nickel/
photoredox catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling reaction for
the allenylation of C(sp
3
)-X bonds using readily available
propargyl carbonates. This methodology operates under very
mild and operationally simple conditions, on the benchtop,
with low loadings of nickel and photocatalyst under visible
light irradiation, and in a nontoxic, sustainable solvent,
acetone. The reaction showcases a broad substrate scope,
encompassing diverse propargyl carbonates and various
primary and secondary alkyl bromides, including elaborated
alkyl bromides.
